title: Some satellite companies still have an appetite for boutique launch services
gist: Germany's Isar Aerospace reached orbit with its Spectrum rocket on its second attempt, and Japanese satellite-servicing firm Astroscale had already signed two launch contracts with Isar before that flight because the 500 kg to 1-ton dedicated-launch segment is nearly empty. Astroscale COO Chris Blackerby disputes the consensus that launch is abundant and cheap, says SpaceX is dialing back Falcon 9 while Starship carries only Starlink, and puts a commercially viable on-orbit servicing ecosystem in the early 2030s.

insights.claim: Satellite operators other than SpaceX broadly say the world still lacks enough capacity to launch payloads into orbit, despite record global launch cadence led by Falcon 9.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: The 'launch is commoditized' narrative is contradicted by the buyers themselves, supporting continued pricing power and funding for new launch entrants.
insights.quote: If you ask most satellite companies aside from SpaceX, they will tell you the world doesn’t have enough capacity for launching payloads into orbit.
insights.locator: If you ask most satellite companies

insights.claim: SpaceX is dialing back its Falcon 9 launch program, and there is no certainty about when Starship will carry anything to orbit other than SpaceX's own Starlink satellites.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: A shrinking Falcon 9 manifest plus a Starlink-only Starship removes the market's assumed capacity cushion and tightens third-party launch supply.
insights.locator: It seems like the customers buying launch services were right

insights.claim: Astroscale's COO says that for all the talk about ubiquitous launch, dropping prices and abundant capacity, he does not see it and there are not a lot of consistently reliable options available.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: A paying customer's direct rebuttal of the launch-glut thesis; reliability, not headline price, is the binding constraint on the satellite market.
insights.quote: for all of the talk about the ubiquity of launch and the dropping prices and the capacity that’s everywhere, I don’t know. I don’t see it yet. There are not a lot of consistently reliable options that are out there.
insights.locator: And when we look around at other options

insights.claim: The 500-kilogram to 1-ton dedicated launch class has thinned out because former contenders including Relativity Space and Astra moved upmarket or exited, leaving Firefly Aerospace's troubled Alpha and few others.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: An underserved mid-small launch niche persists because the industry chased heavier vehicles; a durable pricing pocket for anyone who actually serves it.
insights.quote: But everybody is going bigger now, so there’s not a lot.
insights.locator: That’s exactly right. Our missions are around that area

insights.claim: Uncertainty about how available SpaceX rideshares will be is forcing satellite operators to actively reconsider their launch vehicle options.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Rideshare uncertainty at the dominant provider is the demand catalyst behind new launcher fundraising rounds such as Stoke's.
insights.locator: We’re just excited to see proof

insights.claim: Isar Aerospace's Spectrum rocket reached orbit for the first time from a spaceport in northern Norway, delivering a batch of CubeSats, after its first test flight failed last year.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Europe now has a privately developed orbital launcher outside Arianespace and Avio, a structural change in European access to space.
insights.locator: So it’s no surprise satellite operators are cheering

insights.claim: Government-backed missions from the European Space Agency, the European Union, and the Norwegian and German governments make up the bulk of Isar Aerospace's launch backlog, giving it a captive customer base with an interest in its survival.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Isar's economics are state-underwritten, so its commercial traction should be judged by non-government contracts like Astroscale's, not headline backlog.
insights.locator: Astroscale wasn’t alone in placing early bets

insights.claim: Rocket Factory Augsburg, Spain's PLD Space and the German-French Exploration Company, which is working on a heavy-lift-class rocket engine, are all chasing Isar in the European launch race alongside incumbents Arianespace and Avio.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: European launch is consolidating into a handful of named candidates; Isar's first-mover orbit success likely concentrates capital toward it.
insights.locator: Isar’s success is good news for Europe’s space sector

themes.theme: Buying unproven launch as a calculated risk

insights.claim: Astroscale signed two launch contracts with Isar Aerospace, one announced in March and another days before Isar's first successful orbital flight, committing two of its most important missions to an unproven rocket.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Established operators are now willing to underwrite first-flight launcher risk, which shortens the revenue ramp for new launch companies.
insights.locator: This was the second launch contract Astroscale has inked

insights.claim: Astroscale sent teams to conduct due diligence at Isar Aerospace's manufacturing site and interviewed its technical leaders before committing, treating supplier due diligence like an investment underwriting process.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Factory-level diligence is becoming the standard way customers price launch risk when there is no flight record to rely on.
insights.quote: We had teams go out there to do due diligence research at their manufacturing site and talk to a lot of their technical leaders.
insights.locator: It was Sunday morning, 5 am or so Japan time

insights.claim: Astroscale's missions have outgrown Rocket Lab's Electron on mass, since ADRAS-J fit but ADRAS-J2 and ELSA-M do not, and Rocket Lab's larger Neutron is not ready yet.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Payload mass creep is pushing servicing customers out of small launchers before Neutron arrives, creating a window competitors like Isar can capture.
insights.quote: Right now, for Rocket Lab current capability, we’ve expanded beyond it.
insights.locator: Blackerby: Launch, as you well know

insights.claim: Satellite-servicing business models structurally require dedicated launches rather than rideshares because the spacecraft must reach a specific orbit to meet a specific target satellite.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Servicing demand is inherently dedicated-launch demand, insulating boutique launch providers from rideshare price competition.
insights.locator: Ars: Astroscale’s business case seems to require dedicated launches

insights.claim: US-based Katalyst Space launched in July on Northrop Grumman's seldom-used air-launched Pegasus XL to chase NASA's decaying Swift observatory, but technical problems prevented the rescue.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Scarcity in dedicated launch is pushing customers to obsolete vehicles, and the failed outcome shows the execution risk that carries.
insights.locator: Another satellite servicing company, US-based Katalyst Space

insights.claim: Astroscale's ADRAS-J mission approached and inspected a defunct Japanese H-IIA rocket upper stage within meters in 2024, establishing that a commercial company can rendezvous with a non-communicative, unprepared object.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Proximity operations within meters of an uncooperative target is the technical gate for both debris removal and military inspection markets.
insights.quote: We got to within meters of ADRAS-J.
insights.locator: To be clear, we’re talking about the capability

insights.claim: Imagery from ADRAS-J showed the target rocket body is stably pointing toward Earth, not rotating, and not degraded, which materially de-risks the ADRAS-J2 capture attempt at the payload adapter.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Reconnaissance-then-capture sequencing converts a technology risk into an engineering task, the pattern that makes servicing financeable.
insights.locator: The pictures, which you’ve seen

insights.claim: The ISSA-J1 mission will be harder than ADRAS-J2 because it targets decommissioned satellites with protruding solar arrays that are expected to be spinning, versus a stable oblong rocket body.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Tumbling-target rendezvous is the next capability threshold; success there widens the addressable debris and servicing market dramatically.
insights.locator: Blackerby: ADRAS-J2 is going to an oblong rocket body

insights.claim: Astroscale's ELSA-M spacecraft, led by its UK division, will capture and deorbit a satellite in Eutelsat's OneWeb constellation to demonstrate end-of-life servicing.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: A named commercial constellation operator participating in an end-of-life demo is the first sign of a paying deorbit-service market.
insights.locator: One of Astroscale’s missions assigned to launch

themes.theme: Servicing business model and defense demand

insights.claim: Astroscale's funding model has progressed from fully self-funded (ELSA-D) to jointly funded with JAXA (ADRAS-J) to ESA and UK Space Agency co-funding (ELSA-M), with ADRAS-J2 and most missions going forward described as revenue-positive.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: The equity-burn phase is ending and government contracts now cover mission cost, which is the inflection point for a listed space-services name.
insights.quote: With ADRAS-J2, we’re getting toward being revenue-positive with these missions.
insights.locator: ELSA-D, our first mission, was fully internally funded

insights.claim: Astroscale expects a consistent, commercially viable satellite-servicing ecosystem to begin developing in the early 2030s, and says none of its current eight or nine missions in manufacturing yet amount to repeatable multi-order service.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: A roughly five-plus-year horizon to commercial repeatability sets realistic duration expectations for capital committed to on-orbit servicing.
insights.quote: we’d like to see, by the early part of the next decade, the early 2030s, that we’re going to start seeing a more consistent, commercially viable servicing ecosystem being developed.
insights.locator: I’m assuming you mean like repeatable, consistent servicing

insights.claim: Astroscale has eight or nine missions in manufacturing across its global sites, indicating an order book rather than a single-demo business.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Mission count under manufacturing is the concrete backlog metric to track for a servicing company's revenue ramp.
insights.locator: But the fact is, we’ve got eight, nine missions

insights.claim: Astroscale holds a US Space Force contract for the Provisioner refueling demonstration and sees the strongest demand signal for on-orbit refueling coming from the United States, alongside a Defense Innovation Unit deorbit-as-a-service study and interest in life extension and close-in inspection.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Defense budgets, not commercial operators, are the near-term revenue engine for on-orbit servicing; track Space Force and DIU solicitations as the demand proxy.
insights.quote: We think there’s going to be a growing market for that, and the demand signal is coming in from the US.
insights.locator: Provisioner is big

insights.claim: Government interest in close-in rendezvous and proximity operations is framed around threat characterization, distinguishing station-keeping within meters from flyby imaging at kilometers.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Debris-removal technology is dual-use space situational awareness, which broadens the buyer set and raises export-control and geopolitical sensitivity.
insights.locator: To be clear, we’re talking about the capability
